title: Unveiling the Gastric Phageome: Isolation and Complete Genome Sequencing of Two Novel Helicobacter pylori Bacteriophages
content: Helicobacter (H.) pylori is a Class 1 carcinogen affecting half the global population. In the recent years, spiking emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacterial populations around the world has made treatment of infectious diseases arduous. With the improved understanding of bacteriophage biology, and the availability of its complete genome sequences led to a resurgence of interest in phage therapy as an antimicrobial strategy. The cross-sectional study was enrolled 100 adult patients undergoing elective upper GI endoscopy at Ramadi Teaching Hospital, Iraq. H. pylori was cultured from gastric biopsies under microaerophilic conditions and confirmed by biochemical testing and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Bacteriophages were enriched from filtered gastric juice against a mixed host pool, isolated by spot test and double-layer agar plaque assay, purified to high-titer stocks, and characterized by electron microscopy, host range, efficiency of plating, and chloroform sensitivity. Genomes were sequenced (Illumina iSeq 100), assembled and annotated bioinformatically. H. pylori was isolated from 31/100 patients. Two lytic phages (MBP1, MBP2) were isolated from gastric juice, lysing 83.9% and 77.4% of clinical isolates, respectively, with their cocktail lysing 100%. Both phages were chloroform-sensitive with distinct morphologies by TEM. Their circular genomes (40,704 and 40,666 bp) contained no virulence or resistance genes. VIRIDIC analysis classified MBP1 within an existing genus and MBP2 as a novel genus (GenBank PZ883692, PZ564648). The first isolation and genomic characterization of H. pylori-specific bacteriophages from gastric juice in Iraq. The two phages demonstrated broad, synergistic lytic activity against all clinical isolates, favourable safety profiles free of virulence and resistance genes, and taxonomic novelty, including one representing a potentially novel genus. These findings support gastric bacteriophages as promising, safe candidates for phage-based therapies against H. pylori infection.
